title: After the Pump Handle Came Off, Did the Cholera Stop on Broad Street?
dek: In 1854, on Broad Street in London, the handle of a public pump was removed, and the outbreak faded within days. But the doctor who proposed it warned: don't credit the handle just yet — and the person who completed the chain of evidence was someone who set out to disprove him.

sections.heading: Ten Days, Five Hundred Dead, One Well

paras.t: From 31 August 1854, people were dropping in the streets around Broad Street in Soho, London. Within 250 yards of the point where Cambridge Street meets Broad Street, more than five hundred people died of cholera in ten days; in less than six days the worst-hit streets were deserted by more than three-quarters of their inhabitants.

Dr John Snow fixed on the public pump on the corner. He had no pathogen he could show anyone — only a list of deaths and drinking histories gathered by knocking on doors: 61 of the dead used to drink the Broad Street pump water, 6 could not be traced because everyone connected with them had died or left, and 6 were said not to have drunk it before they fell ill.

The time was early September 1854, the place St James's parish in Westminster, London. Two groups wanted an answer: Snow, the local doctor, who believed the disease came through water; and Whitehead, the curate for the Broad Street area and a member of the parish inquiry committee. The ones who could actually act were the Board of Guardians of St James's parish. There was only one question: was this outbreak connected to that well? The difficulty was that germ theory did not exist yet. All Snow could claim was that the water contained "the cholera poison" — what that substance was, and how it made people ill, nobody could show in physical form.

Snow's method was to look at who was fine. The workhouse in Poland Street was more than three-quarters surrounded by houses in which cholera deaths had occurred, yet only five of its 535 inmates died of cholera — the workhouse had its own pump-well on the premises and never sent to Broad Street for water, and at the death rate of the streets around it more than a hundred people would have died. The brewery on Broad Street, next to the pump, employed over seventy workmen, none of whom suffered severely and only two of whom were mildly indisposed: the men were allowed a certain quantity of malt liquor, and the owner was quite certain that they never obtained water from the pump in the street.

The most striking case was miles away. Mrs E, who lived in Hampstead, had not been near Broad Street for months; she simply preferred that pump's water and had a large bottle brought out each day by the cart that came into the village. The water arrived on Thursday 31 August. She drank some that evening and again on Friday, was seized with cholera on Friday evening, and died on Saturday.

On the evening of 7 September Snow put the circumstances to the Board of Guardians of St James's parish, and the pump handle was removed the next day. But the case curve had already begun to ease: new attacks fell from 143 to 116, then to 54, and by 8 September — the day the handle came off — there were only 12. Snow himself wrote it out clearly: this does not rule out that the water had "ceased to contain the cholera poison". He did not credit the handle.

Meanwhile the Reverend Whitehead had come to knock the theory down. He told a medical friend that he believed a careful investigation would disprove that theory. Going through the parish registers, he noticed a five-month-old girl at 40 Broad Street who had fallen ill on 28 August, earlier than most of the cases. On a visit he learned that the water used to soak the child's napkins had been poured partly into a cesspool in the front area. The later examination confirmed that fluid from the cesspool did percolate into the well. In the end the committee agreed unanimously that the outbreak was "in some manner" attributable to the use of the impure water of the well, but declined to say how it acted. The curate left a line for his own position: "It is far too important a subject to be sacrificed to the symmetry of a theory."

What mattered was less the removal of the handle than the way Snow asked his questions: he did not only ask what the dead had been drinking, he checked what happened to those who had not. The workhouse and the brewery were natural control groups — two populations that stayed away from the well came through the disaster almost untouched. Mrs E ruled out the explanation of place of residence: her only contact was the bottle of water carried out to her.

Whitehead's part matters just as much: a man set on disproving the pump theory supplied the missing link of mechanism himself. The infant fell ill on 28 August and her symptoms stopped on 30 August, before the outbreak's starting point on 31 August, so the sequence of events fits; and the seepage from cesspool to well turned "something in the water" from a guess into a route you could point to. When a sceptic checks the evidence and ends up where his opponents did, that is often worth more than mutual confirmation inside an echo chamber.

But the limits of the evidence need to be stated. Snow's drinking histories came from his own door-to-door visits; six cases could not be checked at all because the families had died or scattered, and under-reporting and recall bias are unavoidable. The removal of the handle and the fall in cases almost coincide, and Snow himself pointed out that there were only 12 new attacks on the day it was removed, so we cannot say that removing the handle ended the outbreak. One explanation is that a one-off contamination fouled the well, the contamination itself had already passed, and the decline happened on its own; removing the handle mainly stopped later people from drinking the remaining water.

sections.heading: How You Can Use It Today

paras.t: Suppose you work for a small delivery-scheduling company, and for three evenings in a row a large share of orders has run late, and everyone suspects the release from the night before last. Don't rush to roll it back: do as Snow did and ask first who was fine — did the two districts with no delays run a different scheduling service? Drawing up a list of the groups that were untouched often finds the boundary faster than staring at the group that broke.

In the review meeting, a colleague who originally wanted to prove it was not the new process dug out earlier logs and found the real trigger. Write up his verification process exactly as it happened, even if the conclusion is unwelcome; and at the same time split the findings into two columns, confirmed and mechanism conjecture, so that a tidy narrative doesn't hide how solid the evidence really is.

This was an observational investigation: no controlled experiment, the sample was the dead, the drinking histories relied on memory, and the well was only one of the shared water sources in the neighbourhood. Today we have lab tests, sequencing and randomised controlled trials, and we do not need to prove anything by removing a handle. The opposite is not always right either: removing the handle first is not always correct — its timing sits almost on top of a natural decline, and what it prevented was more likely repeated drinking afterwards. Also, don't write it up as a lone-hero story: the mechanism link was supplied by someone who wanted to disprove him.

reflection.scenario: Fictional situation: three stores of a bakery chain receive customer complaints of diarrhoea over the same weekend, and the company first suspects a batch of cream; store A has already stopped using that batch, yet sporadic complaints continue. The quality manager in charge of purchasing first wants to prove that the cream is not at fault.
reflection.question: Before the lab results come back, on what evidence would you stop using this batch of cream and notify customers, or stay silent? The cost of stopping is destroying stock and admitting a risk; the cost of not stopping is that more people may be harmed — which mistake do you think is harder to undo?

example.assumptions: Assume the number of cases is still small and causation is unconfirmed, but that batch of cream really does cover all three stores; assume that a public notice would trigger a regulatory reporting process.
example.steps: First list who was fine: are there similar complaints from stores or product lines that did not use this batch; check whether the onset times come after the batch arrived; ask a colleague who does not want the settled conclusion to review the orders and production records independently; set a trigger line for temporary withdrawal, for example stopping the batch as soon as a second case linked to it appears.
example.alternative: Another reasonable choice is to withdraw the batch only at store A on a small scale, keep samples for testing, and not make a public notice for now: the reason is that the evidence is still weak and this avoids wrong attribution and panic; the cost is that a wrong call delays action.

uncertainty_note: Most of the main events and figures come from Snow's own 1855 book and his report to the committee (B-E1 to B-E9), so there is a single-source problem. The 61/6/6 drinking histories come from Snow's door-to-door visits and may contain under-reporting; six cases could not be checked at all. The case of Mrs E (B-E9) was relayed by her son and is second-hand information from a single source. Whitehead's statement that he initially wanted to disprove the pump theory (B-E10) comes from the recollection in his own report and cannot be checked against other accounts. The conclusion that fluid from the cesspool seeped into the well (B-E13) comes from the committee's investigation, and no specific test method is recorded. The removal of the handle and the fall in cases coincide in time, so causation cannot be established; Snow himself had noted that there were only 12 new attacks on 8 September, and he did not rule out that the water had already ceased to contain the causative substance (B-E6, B-E8). In 1854 there was no modern germ theory; Snow used the expression "the cholera poison". The committee only said the outbreak was "in some manner" attributable to the impure water of the well and explicitly expressed no opinion on the mode of action (B-E14, B-E15). This piece did not obtain the view of the central health authority on this matter, so its position is not given.
